questions.question: Build the fixed assets note for the equipment and name its three agreements.
questions.expected_answer: Opening carrying value nil (bought this year); additions at cost R18 000; depreciation for the year R1 800; closing carrying value R16 200, presented as cost R18 000 less accumulated depreciation R1 800. Agreements: the closing carrying value equals the statement of financial position's fixed assets line; the year's depreciation charge equals the income statement's depreciation expense; and the asset register stands behind the note as the item-level detail.

questions.question: Build the four working-capital notes and the owner's equity note, with totals.
questions.expected_answer: Inventories: trading stock R2 250 + consumable stores on hand R200 = R2 450. Trade and other receivables: trade debtors R3 850 + accrued income R500 + prepaid expenses R600 = R4 950. Cash and cash equivalents: bank R15 000 + petty cash R300 = R15 300. Trade and other payables: trade creditors R3 200 + accrued expenses R100 + income received in advance R500 = R3 800. Owner's equity: opening R20 000 + contributions nil + net profit R7 900 − drawings R4 000 = closing R23 900. Every total must agree with its statement line to the rand.

questions.question: Explain the connection the syllabus draws between formal statements and indigenous bookkeeping.
questions.expected_answer: Stokvels, burial societies and savings clubs have kept trusted records for generations — contribution registers, member pages, payout rosters — sharing the same architecture as formal accounting: member-by-member detail agreeing with a running total (a control account and its list in another form) and full transparency to every stakeholder. Both traditions solve the universal problem that money held for others must be accounted to them in detail, on demand; GAAP and the stokvel book are two languages for the same honesty, and both punish a total that cannot survive the member's check.
